bib.title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research", Starace, Jaffe, Sherburn, Aung, Chan, Maksin, Dias, Mays, Kinsella, Thompson, Heidecke, Glaese, Patwardhan (OpenAI). Venue as printed: "Pre-print. Copyright 2025 by the author(s)."; arXiv:2504.01848v3 [cs.AI], 7 Apr 2025. No conference venue is printed on the PDF.

COVERAGE: 30 of 30 pages, 103,565 of 103,565 chars. Body (p1-10), appendices A-I (p13-30), all per-paper result tables and all prompt figures were read in full. References (p10-12) were skimmed for origins only. The note 06-evaluating-agents.md has no existing PaperBench mention (grep for "paperbench" and "2504.01848" returned nothing).

CLAIMS

- claim: The rubric is a weighted tree; only leaves are graded, pass/fail, and a parent's score is the weighted average of its children up to the root.
  number: 8,316 leaf nodes across 20 papers (I summed Table 7's leaf column and it matches)
  setup: 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight/Oral papers; each rubric co-developed with an original author; weights mean importance, not difficulty; the agent never sees the rubric
  quote: "Leaf nodes are graded for binary pass/fail criteria, and a parent's score is the weighted average of its children." (p3, Fig. 2) / "Across the 20 papers in PaperBench there are 8,316 leaf nodes." (p5)
  where: p3, p5, Table 7 p15

- claim: Leaves are decomposed until one is quick for an expert to check.
  number: under 15 minutes per leaf
  setup: design rule, assumes familiarity with the paper
  quote: "an expert human could review whether a submission satisfies it in less than 15 minutes" (p5)
  where: p5

- claim: There are three leaf types (Code Development, Execution, Result Match), each showing the judge different files. Result Match is graded only from outputs of a fresh re-run of reproduce.sh on a clean VM, not from the agent's own run.
  number: none
  setup: Ubuntu 24.04 VM, A10 GPU; reproduce.sh capped at 12 hours in their experiments, average run 5.5 minutes
  quote: "ensure replication outputs can be distinguished from any results hard-coded by the candidate at task-time" (p3)
  where: p3-4, Table 1

- claim: The judge (SimpleJudge) grades each leaf independently, given the paper, addendum, sibling/ancestor criteria and the top-ranked relevant files. It was validated on JudgeEval, a set of human-graded leaves.
  number: o3-mini-high F1 0.83 (accuracy 0.83, precision 0.83, recall 0.83) at $66 per paper; o1 F1 0.84 at $830; GPT-4o 0.73 at $120; GPT-4o-mini 0.59 at $8; random 0.49
  setup: JudgeEval = partial replications of four PaperBench papers plus one dev-set paper, hand-graded by the authors; macro-averaged across papers; binary classification per leaf
  quote: "o3-mini with the SimpleJudge scaffolding is the most cost-effective, with an F1 score of 0.83 at $66 USD per paper" (p6)
  where: p6, Table 3

- claim: Judge accuracy differs by leaf type; it is weakest on judging code and strongest on matching results.
  number: o3-mini-high F1 0.72 Code Development, 0.82 Execution, 0.94 Result Match
  setup: same JudgeEval
  quote: "O3- MINI -HIGH achieves an F1-score of 0.72 in Code Development, which we deem acceptable for tracking signal on this requirement type." (p18)
  where: p18, Table 8

- claim: Grading cost in tokens, and against a human grader.
  number: about 50M input and 2M output tokens per paper; human estimated at 12 hours at $100/hr
  setup: o3-mini judge; the human figure is an assumed rate, not a measured bill
  quote: "On average SimpleJudge uses around 50,000,000 input tokens and 2,000,000 output tokens per paper." (p6, fn 7) / "Human cost estimated at 12 hours of work at an hourly rate of $100 USD/hr." (p17, Fig. 5)
  where: p6, p17

- claim: Running the agents costs far more than grading them.
  number: $400 per paper, $8,000 per 20-paper run; grading adds $66 per paper
  setup: o1 IterativeAgent, 12-hour rollout, API credits only
  quote: "it costs $400 in API credits to run an o1 IterativeAgent 12-hour rollout on a single paper in PaperBench. For the 20 papers, this sums to $8000 USD per eval run." (p9)
  where: p9

- claim: Human baseline: ML PhDs beat o1 on a 3-paper subset, and the agent leads early then plateaus.
  number: humans 41.4% (best of 3 attempts, 48 hours) vs o1 26.6%
  setup: 8 participants enrolled in or holding an ML PhD; 4 papers attempted, 3 attempts each, only the best performer after week one was extended; part-time over four weeks, hours from a timesheet with unattended compute time counted; AI assistants allowed; o1 with IterativeAgent, 36-hour run
  quote: "our human baseline of ML PhDs (best of 3 attempts) achieved 41.4% after 48 hours of effort, compared to 26.6% achieved by o1 on the same subset" (p2)
  where: p2, p8, Fig. 3

- claim: Headline agent scores, and their sensitivity to scaffold.
  number: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 21.0 ± 0.8, o1 13.2 ± 0.3 (BasicAgent); with IterativeAgent o1 24.4 ± 0.7, Claude 16.1 ± 0.1; o1 at 36 hours 26.0 ± 0.3
  setup: 20 papers, 3 runs each, 12-hour limit, A10 GPU, o3-mini judge; error is one SEM
  quote: "We observe that these modifications significantly boost scores for o3-mini and o1 compared to BasicAgent, but hamper Claude 3.5 Sonnet, highlighting models' sensitivities to prompting." (p7, Table 5)
  where: p7, Tables 4-5

- claim: Scores come almost entirely from writing code, not from running it or matching results.
  number: Claude BasicAgent 35.4 Code Dev / 1.8 Execution / 0.7 Result; best@3 human 72.4 / 20.4 / 8.9
  setup: Table 9; human row is the 3-paper subset
  quote: "BEST @3 H UMAN [3 PAPER SUBSET ] 72.4 20 .4 8 .9" (p19)
  where: p19

- claim: The code-only variant is cheaper but only a weak proxy for the full benchmark.
  number: Pearson r 0.48; grading about $10 per paper (about 85% less); o1 scores 43.4 ± 0.8
  setup: o1 only
  quote: "o1 performance correlates with a Pearson r value of 0.48, with PB = 0.45PBCD + 0.05." (p4, fn 5)
  where: p4, p6, Table 6

- claim: A coarser rubric inflates the score. Collapsing the tree to shallower depths raised one submission's grade sharply.
  number: 0.93 (1 leaf), 0.48 (9 leaves), 0.30 (30), 0.27 (90), 0.25 (361, unpruned); depth 3 cut grading cost 10x
  setup: a single JudgeEval submission ("rice/0"), 3 repeats, experimental judge
  quote: "pruning at depth 3 reduced grading cost by 10×, while the performance of the Judge deteriorates only slightly" (p18)
  where: p18-19, Fig. 6

- claim: Rule violations were caught by a log text search plus manual review.
  number: 10 of 646 runs disqualified, scored 0
  quote: "We find 10 cases of using blacklisted resources across all 646 runs" (p4)
  where: p4

- claim: Run-to-run variance on the same paper is high.
  number: none overall; e.g. o3-mini IterativeAgent on one paper scored 0.680, 0.542, 0.144 (p22, Table 14)
  quote: "Due to the high variance, we recommend others to use several seeds when evaluating PaperBench" (p18)
  where: p18

LIMITS
- Conceded: only 20 papers; the judge "is not as accurate as an expert human" and is non-deterministic; rubrics take "multiple weeks per paper" and others were hard to train to write them; contamination risk for future models; loopholes "cannot yet" be ruled out; no adversarial stress test of the judge.
- Not shown: no inter-rater agreement for the human gold labels (the human is treated as ideal performance); the number of JudgeEval submissions and leaves is not stated; JudgeEval submissions were human-made, partly from authors' code, so judge accuracy on real agent output is untested; no judge repeat-variance figure on the main results; no measure of how judge error shifts the final Replication Score; no trajectory grading at all, since it is outcome and artifact grading only; no comparison against alternative rubrics, though the authors say "many different realizations" would be "no less valid".
- Human baseline: 8 people, 3 papers, best-of-3 with selective extension, assigned to papers they felt most confident on, AI tools allowed; four attempts used an A100 instead of an A10. It is not a clean human-only or average-human number.
- Dated: models are Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1, o3-mini, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash and DeepSeek-R1, with prices as of 2025/03/21. Authors say results are not an upper bound.

BUILDS ON: Rubrics: Sawada et al., 2023 (ARB); Harvey Team, 2024 (BigLaw Bench). LLM judges: Zheng et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2023; Zhuge et al., 2024 (Agent-as-a-Judge). Benchmarks: Siegel et al., 2024 (CORE-Bench); Chan et al., 2024 (MLE-bench); Wijk et al., 2024 (RE-Bench, credited for the agents-lead-early pattern). Scaffold: Yao et al., 2023 (ReAct); UK AI Safety Institute, 2025 (Inspect basic agent).

CODE: Judge output structure, p27 Fig. 9: "# Expectations ... # Reality ... # Score ... Give a score of either 0 or 1" and "If anything appears to be missing, assume that the attempt failed to produce it (treat it as a failure)."

FIGURES: Figure 2, p3, "Rubrics hierarchically decompose the replication task into a tree of increasingly granular requirements..." It shows weights, binary leaves and the roll-up to 55% in one picture, which is the mechanism the note needs. (Runner-up if cost matters more: Fig. 5, p17, judge F1 against cost per paper.)

PROBLEMS
- Extraction was clean. Figure-internal text for Figs. 1-3 and 6 is scrambled, and the human-judge value in Fig. 6 is not recoverable from the text.
- The PDF reproduces judge, agent and task prompts in full (p25-30), with imperative text such as "You are judging..." and "YOU MUST use the bash and python tools". I treated these as exhibits and did not follow them.
- Internal inconsistencies in the source: footnote 7 prices the o3-mini judge on "public OpenAI o1 API pricing"; the reproduce.sh cap is 12 hours in the text (p3) but "7 days" in the task instructions (p29); Table 9 says o1 IterativeAgent used two seeds while Table 12 lists three runs; Table 9 labels the third column "Results Analysis" rather than Result Match; Table 17's FRE row (0*, 0*, 0.007, mean 0.061) does not add up; the abstract says "20 ICML 2024" papers and Fig. 3 covers 4 papers while the headline human number is on 3.
